finding: Strong community-specific evidence exists for an article distinguishing remembered migration from documented household craft, and showing that inherited knowledge changes with work and markets. No universal caste creation date or founder established. Three inspected sources suffice; do not transfer generic Tanti or all-weaver biography into Bhulia identity.

sources.title: R.V.Russell, assisted by Rai Bahadur Hira Lal, The Tribes and Castes of the Central Provinces of India, VolumeII
sources.locator: Bhulia entry, HTMLlines3680–3696; footnote identifies paper taken by Hira Lal at Sonpur.
sources.inspection: Actual full historical entry and title-page transcription inspected, not search snippets.
sources.claims: The entry records a tradition of migration with the first Chauhan Raja of Patna, explicitly as one tradition. It speculates about northern connections rather than documenting a dated journey. It describes exogamous vansa groups, with some names linked to villages, and records competing explanations of the community name. Its hostile origin sayings and ranking language demonstrate why colonial categorisation cannot be accepted as ancestry. Useful sentence: a migration tradition was already recorded in1916; that dates the written record, not the migration.
sources.strength: Original colonial-era ethnographic witness, based on named Sonpur contributor; evidence of what was recorded, not proof that tradition happened.
limits: Exclude abusive proverbs, purity/rank assertions and innate-trait stereotypes.
Do not turn author speculation linking Koshta/Devang into modern alias or common-ancestry claim.
No current marriage practice inferred from1916description.
1901population decrease follows boundary transfer; not population collapse.

sources.title: Jyotirmayee Acharya, Gendered Spaces: Craftswomen’s Stories of Self-Employment in Orissa, India
sources.publication: NTNU Dr.polit.thesis2004:74; ISBN82-471-6361-6 electronic. Cover says2003, formal titlepage2004.
sources.locator: Printed75/PDF96 named Tulasi Meher interview;80–81/PDF101–102 household production and women;Appendix3 printed236/PDF150 fieldwork timeline;table printed50/PDF71 Barhamunda participant identified Bhulia.
sources.inspection: Original thesis PDF text inspected; public mirror, institutional publication identifiable in titlepages. Interview names may be study names, not independently identity-checked living individuals.
sources.claims: Tulasi Meher and her husband in Barhamunda describe weaving for local consumers across generations, followed by wider markets. The thesis separately identifies Bhulia and Kustha communities. Asked how production continued with only men visible as registered workers, Bhulia/Kustha respondents stressed capable household members, not simply male numbers. Acharya documents women's starch preparation, reeling and tie-dye work and difficulty gaining independent registration/finance. These are observations from her fieldwork period, not claims about every present household. Work credited to one registered weaver could depend on several people's labour.
sources.strength: Original doctoral fieldwork with interviews, participant tables and methodology.
limits: Fieldwork appendix gives1998–99,2000–01 and2002revisits; exact date for each interview not stated.
Women's work passage spans several named weaving localities/groups; do not call every described worker Bhulia.
No caste inferred solely from Meher surname; use explicit participant/community context.
Do not reproduce photographs without licence.

sources.title: Bedaprakash Narayan Tanty, Emerging Trends on Indigenous Knowledge of a Weaving Community in Sonepur District, Odisha
sources.publication: Saudi Journal of Humanities and Social Sciences6(11),461–467,24November2021; DOI10.36348/sjhss.2021.v06i11.002
sources.locator: p462study area/methods;pp462–463instruments and specialised work;pp463–464learning to weave.
sources.inspection: Actual original7pagePDF and journal metadata inspected.
sources.claims: Research selected six Bhulia-dominated villages in and around Sonepur, using interviews, group discussion and observation. It describes family-guided learning alongside winding machines, drum, jacquard/dobby attachments and synthetic dyes. Specialised tasks and links to master weavers changed the earlier household organisation. Its central useful insight is that inherited skill adapts: new tools can expand designs and production while dependence on finance and masters can reduce control. This is a reported local study, not a census of all Bhulia households.
sources.strength: Original field-study article with methods; less fully specified sample than desirable.
limits: Six villages not individually named in inspected study-area section; sample count and fieldwork dates unclear.
Do not repeat general StoneAge/3000year antiquity claims as Bhulia origin.
No universal claim that all natural dyes vanished or all weavers became wage labourers.
PDF licence saysCCBY-NC4.0; no images recommended for site reuse without fit assessment.
